sn12.18:1.2: Then the wanderer Timbaruka approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him.
sn12.18:1.3: When they had concluded their greetings and cordial talk, he sat down to one side and said to him:
sn12.18:2.1: “How is it, Master Gotama: are pleasure and pain created by oneself?”
sn12.18:2.2: “Not so, Timbaruka,” the Blessed One said.
sn12.18:2.3: “Then, Master Gotama, are pleasure and pain created by another?”
sn12.18:2.4: “Not so, Timbaruka,” the Blessed One said.
sn12.18:2.5: “How is it then, Master Gotama: are pleasure and pain created both by oneself and by another?”
sn12.18:2.6: “Not so, Timbaruka,” the Blessed One said.
sn12.18:2.7: “Then, Master Gotama, have pleasure and pain arisen fortuitously, being created neither by oneself nor by another?”
sn12.18:2.8: “Not so, Timbaruka,” the Blessed One said.
sn12.18:2.9: “How is it then, Master Gotama: is there no pleasure and pain?”
sn12.18:2.10: “It is not that there is no pleasure and pain, Timbaruka; there is pleasure and pain.”
sn12.18:2.11: “Then is it that Master Gotama does not know and see pleasure and pain?”
sn12.18:2.13: “It is not that I do not know and see pleasure and pain, Timbaruka.
sn12.18:3.1: “Whether you are asked: ‘How is it, Master Gotama: are pleasure and pain created by oneself?’
sn12.18:3.3: or ‘Are they created by another? ’ or ‘Are they created by both?’ or ‘Are they created by neither?’ in each case you say: ‘Not so, Timbaruka.’
sn12.18:3.5: When you are asked: ‘How is it then, Master Gotama: is there no pleasure and pain?’ you say: ‘It is not that there is no pleasure and pain, Timbaruka; there is pleasure and pain.’
sn12.18:3.7: When asked: ‘Then is it that Master Gotama does not know and see pleasure and pain?’ you say: ‘It is not that I do not know and see pleasure and pain, Timbaruka.
sn12.18:3.10: Venerable sir, let the Blessed One explain pleasure and pain to me.
sn12.18:3.11: Let the Blessed One teach me about pleasure and pain.”
sn12.18:4.1: “Timbaruka, if one thinks, ‘The feeling and the one who feels it are the same,’ then one asserts with reference to one existing from the beginning: ‘Pleasure and pain are created by oneself.’ I do not speak thus.
sn12.18:4.2: But, Timbaruka, if one thinks, ‘The feeling is one, the one who feels it is another,’ then one asserts with reference to one stricken by feeling: ‘Pleasure and pain are created by another.’ Neither do I speak thus.
sn12.18:4.3: Without veering towards either of these extremes, the Tathagata teaches the Dhamma by the middle:
sn12.18:4.4: ‘With ignorance as condition, volitional formations come to be;
sn12.18:4.5: with volitional formations as condition, consciousness….
sn12.18:4.6: Such is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.
sn12.18:4.7: But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance comes cessation of volitional formations; with the cessation of volitional formations,
sn12.18:4.9: Such is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.’”
sn12.18:5.1: When this was said, the naked ascetic Timbaruka said to the Blessed One:
sn12.18:5.3: I go for refuge to Master Gotama, and to the Dhamma, and to the Bhikkhu Saṅgha.
sn12.18:5.4: From today let Master Gotama remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”
